reviews.review: Great game, interesting and engaging for a low price.

While the game is beautiful and handcrafted I cannot recommend it due to a bug in the game that risks a potential hazard to your computer hardware.

1st: the game keeps generating new internet permission requests in my firewall which io keep denying.
A single player game has no buisness attempting to connect to the internet.

2nd there are cases that when upon denying these requests the game will cause some weird IRQ conflict error that crashes your graphics card. (I will also note that i never had a game cause an IRQ conflict upon denying an internet request via my firewall before, this game is the first game i encountered to cause such a thing)

I have a threadripper 1950x and an RTX 2080TI, when I tried to launch the game after it crashed to desktop, it crashed to desktop again. and all my other games expirenced the same issue even though the graphics card was still registered in my system. but during these crashes my fan speeds would reset to default.

upon rebooting i could play everything normally again and then when I launched orwell again and denied the new internet request, crash to desktop, and persistent crashes in every other game till i rebooted.

I dont know why a single player game needs an internet connection, or what its doing that is causing an IRQ conflict so bad that it crashes my graphics card.

But i cannot recommend this game in good faith because of the severity of the crash it causes. it may not happen every time, nor will it likey happen on every system configuration but I refuse to recommend a game that causes an IRQ conflict on ANY system for ANY reason.

A very unique and interesting game.
Has a social commentary about mass surveillance by governmental organisations such as NSA, FBI and MI5.

This is something that should be on everyone's mind in 2019 and beyond. With the threat of terror and attacks though out the world, freedom of speech has been attacked and the idea of `thought crimes' are becoming a real thing.

In short a very interesting game, choices do in fact matter.

Its nice the game does not have any "PC" overtones and does in fact have a place for both types of people, the people who believe Government organisations should have the power to access private information about everything you have ever done or said online. 
And for the people who do not think they should.

It gets really addictive spying on those people.  The game will punish you if you blindly click on anything highlighted, which ends up being good because it helps you pay attention and think.  I want to work for the CIA now...

I found the story is engaging enough, and the game explores some interesting concepts and questions. Many of the themes have already been thoroughly explored in a variety of philosophical sci-fi / dystopian plots, but the gameplay made me feel involved, and the not-too-distant, not-so-different-future setting instilled a teensy bit of discomforting familiarity with the game world.

Obviously if you're not into decision-focused, plot- and character-centered games or not a fan of story-telling primarily through pictures and text, this game might not be your dig.

Disclaimer, i got this game for free from some giveaway, though even if I didnt i doubt my opinion would change much because my concept of price-to-quality probably needs some work. Basically you can more or less take this as a review without worrying about if i got it for free.

TL;DR at bottom if you want that.

Orwell is... well an Orwellian game (I think i'm using that right). You are more or less the disembodied investigator (with a face and directly spoken to though) that is responsible for keeping tabs on several people, and uncover the story of a recent bombing in a (probably) realistic surveillance state (or whatever its called exactly). It's not a blatant dystopia where the government is paranoid of everyone, its a much more gray area, where everyone lives generally normal lives, but should the need arise the government can quickly go through everything they have online. 

Day 1: investigate connection of one citizen to a bombing. Is it coincidence they have a police record and happen to be leaving the area barely a minute before the bomb goes off?  

Day 2: things go from bad to worse. I'm not going to go farther, but it goes from "uncover truth of a recent tragedy" to "[i]make sure any tragedies are prevented, [b]at all costs[/b][/i]"

The game's art style is really good, though there is the awkward/uncanny face photos every once in a while, but generally are pretty good.

The main music loop is good. Its not amazing, but it doesn't get annoying. Some of the musical stingers are a bit on the nose, but at the same time i often get chills from them, even the relieving ones. Not many scores do that so regularly. they can sometimes sorta spoil some of the twists, but usually just by a few seconds, at most. Even then, its basically saying "[i]read carefully motherf***er, there are lives on the line with this one, [b]dont f*ck this up[/b] [/i]"

The game overall is sorta short (single digit hours, but more than one sitting, unless you plan to speed through it in a day, which i do NOT recommend, this is a game you take your time on, see last line of above paragraph) with not much replay value by itself, but I came back to it after a few months, mostly fresh after forgetting many of the exact details (with all the info you collect, some of the bits are bound to be"unloaded" by your brain)

TL;DR, a slow and well paced thinking game, unique art, good main theme and heavy hitting moments. 9/10. Worth a few dollars, imo (though again not the best judgement for that).

Just remember, your actions have consequences. [i][b]Don't screw it up

This is a beautiful game engine and fantastic and engaging story, ruined by a shitty ending that artificial constraints force you into. Yes, there are alternate endings but you have to play through the whole game again to find them, and also explicitly ignore the things that the game itself expects you to do; you're now gaming the game design, not playing the game.

It's a shame. I had a great experience and now it's utterly ruined because they couldn't close it off.

The mystery itself is interesting and entertaining, but the real value here is thinking about surveillance and information - I found it very difficult to maintain appropriate boundaries for what was "relevant" to the investigation or not. Mental states? Blog posts? Divorces? It certainly makes it difficult to want to endorse human judgment as the right way to make these decisions, except that also that also your own judgment is what makes things turn out better (and it's not obvious that strict rules would do a better job). So it gives you a lot to think about.

In one of the classes I'm taking at the university I'm attending we were required to study the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, Edward Snowden, and a few other things relating to that. And the more I see the more I begin to realize that this game is scary accurate to the real thing. From everything I can tell this is almost exactly what it's like to be a part of the real thing from how information is collected, to how everyone you know becomes a target, to even how [spoiler] it's revealed that even you are being monitored [/spoiler]. At the same time though it asks all these brilliant questions that make you question even whether it's better to possibly give up your privacy, your own thoughts for a bit of extra security, as you go around monitoring people's knowing what you're doing is wrong you can't help but feel like you've done the right thing when you actually save the lives of more people, and prevent additional terror attacks.

This game is scary accurate to the real thing, and if you care even remotely for your privacy you need to give this game a chance.

*TL;DR AT BOTTOM* 
Firstly I'd just like to say I'm not one to review games often, but I'll give it a shot. I'll give a little overview of my view, a summary of how the game works, some of the pros, the cons, who I'd recommend the game for, and then a final rating.

So I've just finished playing through one run of the game, well doing one run through of it and I have to say I've really enjoyed it. It's incredibly well designed, with a brilliant branching storyline which you have a direct effect on. Admittedly it only has a few hours of playing if you only want to do the one run through, but if you're even more of a completionist than I am there is some replayablity, as the different choices you make influence the development of the situation, who gets arrested, who is charged with what, through to the political outcomes.

Basically the game focuses on a network of people who are implicated after a bomb goes off, and you play the role of an investigator, who has the job of going through various news sources, private files, phone calls, social media communications etc, and choosing what datachunks to process, in order to solve the various tasks you are presented with. Sometimes you might face conflicting bits of data, and it's down to you to choose what to process, this can be based on ignorant sources, or particular context of the sources. 

As mentioned, the storyline that you can influence is particularly interesting, and the general depth to the characters and plot is quite phenomenal. The game itself runs very easily, and though overall you are a little guided with what to look at, this fits with the overall design of the surveillance system you are a part of. I particularly like the flexibility you have, in that if you want you can be like me and just read through loads of different material which might not even help you, but can immerse you in the setting. Further, there were one or two moments where I was wondering what should I do next, but as it all turned out I had overlooked or forgot about particular things, so it's not too complex, but does require a little thought.

In terms of negatives, there's not too much to complain about. In terms of the game, maybe the ability to load up the game on the different days or after each task is done, particularly towards the end of the story, would be good, in order to just look at the different endings without a full replay. I loved the story, and look forward to playing the next game, but I still would have loved if the game had been longer. Which brings me to the price, at £7.19, for only 4 hours content (well for me anyway with only one run through), the game might be a little steep, but I really enjoyed it to be honest, and if you see it in a sale, go for it.

Overall I'm going to say the game itself is a 9/10, very well designed, but the experience as a whole is more a 7/10 due to the limited playtime for the price. Long review for sure, but hope it helped. Enjoy your day!

TL;DR: Well designed game with branching/influenceable story, deep setting, drawing on relevant themes with surveillance, government, and freedom vs security, unique game type, quite a price for relatively short amount of playtime, deffo worth on sale, 9/10 game itself, 7/10 factoring in price and content.

This game as the name might imply borrows it's broad strokes from the novel 1984. If you haven't read the book you can still enjoy the game even though you won't get a bunch of references. in the game you play an investigator who is tasked with solving a terrorist attack.  This is done by Facebook stalking. people this works by you reading a Facebook profile for example. and uploading certain phrases which are highlighted into the system. Doing this will unlock new source of information allowing you to get the complete picture. This mechanic is fun though not perfect since the game only allows you to draw a particular conclusion when you get the specific line that allows one to do so rather then taking everything you have seen into account. i feel this game would have worked better if it allowed you to type the conclusions you came to into the system yourself in a text adventure like setup. However i understand why the developer didn't go this route. This doesn't mean its just a matter of uploading whatever is highlighted since you can choose what information you put in the system and what you leave out. your decisions on every piece of information can effect how the game plays out.  No matter what route you take the investigation is very absorbing this is aided by the color's and the very minimalist art which has to grow on you but helps you focus on the story.  the same minimalism applies to the use of music but damn it works.  The biggest negative i have against the game is that once you know the story replay can be a bit meh since the big twist is always the same. However i found fun in changing the story to get all the achievements and to see all the different endings. i'm not sure if my playtime is actually as long as steam says i think i left the game on once TBH. however for 10 ish bucks you'll have a good time especially if you try and get all the achievements. i wish i could tell you more but get this game and enjoy a cool investigation with a good message about how data can be used and abused.

Orwell is a pretty engaging game with an interesting narrative, which drives the player to consider the ramifications of a surveillance state. You come to find that if you dig enough, anyone can become the guilty party. The mechanic of pulling text "data chunks" out of the social media posts and news articles in order to piece together a profile for each suspect is definitely interesting. The game makes you feel like you really could be just a participant in the spying program. It's probably not for everyone, but I found myself doing a chapter (there are 5) daily until I was done, and the time went by quick. The story has a good payoff, and the mystery it unravels is very compelling. I'd say if you're on the fence, give it a try.

To start this review, I would like to mention that I am a massive fan of Orwell, both author and game. I found this game shortly after reading the novel this game is based on, Nineteen Eighty-Four. And let me tell you, it sure does scratch the Orwell itch. Playing the game I truly felt put in the role of a member of the Party, demanding subservience over the serfs of the Nation and ensuring it's complete control. The story is a very interesting and engaging detective drama with, while not very deep, enjoyable characters as well as unique moments. The gameplay has you scour through newspapers, dating profiles, texts, dms, websites, having you discern useful information for your investigation, including having you choose between conflicting information. What's really interesting about this game, however, is it's branching paths you can take based on what information you choose to add and omit, leading to different outcomes for the people whose lives you essentially control. There are multiple distinct endings and several different ways you can get to them that makes this game worth replaying (unless you're like me, who chooses to replay the game and get the same ending [spoiler] Long live Oceania! 2+2=5! Ignorance Is Strength! [/spoiler].) both of my playthroughs took me around 3 hours, and with at least 3 distinct endings, that's about 9 hours of total play time, if'n you're so inclined as to get each ending. So I'd say, if you're a fan of George Orwell, detective stories, dystopia, or some healthy social and political commentary, I'd say this is the game for you. If you aren't into any of those, I'd pick the game up on sale, it's a good story for a rainy day. If I were a professional rate this game an 8/10, but personally, the game is a 10/10.

This a pretty clever little narrative game. 

You essentially play the role of an investigator using a survelliance software system called Orwell, and investigate people that are citizens of a country referred to as "The Nation", that seems to be modeled off of present day Western nations like the US, UK, Canada etc. You don't have total access to everything, as your adviser often needs to 'get clearance' to add someone to the target list, but you still wield a chilling amount of investigative power eventually. 

This is not set in an extreme totalitarian world like the state of Oceania in [i]1984[/i], but a mostly present day world. It's a bit ambiguous though, as a couple real countries are referred to eventually, and 'The Nation' has some ominous things about it that suggest a veiled totalitarianism, especially with references to 'The Party'.  

There isn't alot of 'gameplay' to it, as you basically just use the mouse to collect bits of information on people from your various electronic sources. It's UI is basically the same ideas as using a computer and web browser.  

While all selectable information is highlighted for you, you do have to make decisions about what information to upload to a person's Orwell profile, and that can have major consequences for events in the story.  Some info is obviously useful, some is just mundane, some bits of info conflict with others. With the conflicting info though, i wish there were sometimes more avaliable info to make a better judgement, but I guess that's the point. 

There are at least a few different endings, but you may have to do a full playthrough again to get them, i'm not sure. 

Without giving away any spoilers to the story, there is a persistent (and i'm sure intentional) irony about the people you are tasked to investigate.  The in-game stated purpose of Orwell and your position is to protect the nation from terrorist threats.  The story starts off when a small bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza.  From that point, the network of people you investigate are all tied to the ideology of wanting privacy. Basically, you are doing the exact things that are fueling this ideology. 

This is excellent social and political commentary in the form of a simple game, and I would definitetly recommend it!

An amazing piece of commentary on encroaching surveillance tech and how woefully susceptible it is to misuse, misinterpretation and bad faith justification using poor or skewed implementation. 

Some say you have nothing to fear if you have nothing to hide, but the game asks, what if you should be afraid of those looking?

[h1] "For The Nation, for the security of the citizens, for their safety, I shall be the investigator. The one who shall observe and... eliminate." [/h1]

What is in this mysterious name: Orwell? A good plot? Realism and coherence? A branching storyline? Memorable characters? Plot twists? Perhaps, all of the mentioned and a lot more? Yes - all of the mentioned and A LOT more. This game is a very interesting game in which you'll act as an investigator working for a governmental project called "Orwell." With the help of this mass surveillance software/tool, you will be tracking and evaluating various people to identify potential "threats" to The Nation. The evaluation process includes analyzing social media accounts of the people evaluated, their chat histories, emails, phone calls, personal devices, and etc. Basically anything, which they deemed a part of their "private" life. 

What I really liked about this game is its attention to detail. On the first look, the game's storyline contains lots of unnecessary snippets of information, which might be regarded as useless by the inattentive player. However, those little details and discrepancies form a larger picture which reveals a major plot twist that takes place somewhere in the ending episodes. The plot twist itself [spoiler], which was about Juliet being the imposter instead of the suspected Harrison,[/spoiler]did make sense after some other playthroughs (accomplishing all the achievements and endings) as I've paid a lot of attention to those little details in the game. [spoiler]For me, the hint provided by Symes about Juliet's favorite book (The Mockingbird)and Harrison's lost phone seemed like the ones which can directly lead you towards the "Juliet is the true imposter" conclusion. [/spoiler]Well, the game proved to me that no story can be regarded as completely explored without the consideration of all the small details. A lesson well learnt.

As much as I liked this game, there are still things that can be improved. For instance, adding a setting for an accelerated playthrough, because DAMN, some of the calls take more than 10 minutes to finish and are unskippable. Going through the game again becomes a real pain without this feature. I understand that some events happen during phone calls (which is probably why you can't accelerate them), but as a person who finished the main plot multiple times, I don't bother to read all the stuff again. Besides, I think players decide beforehand their choices, so adding the accelerated playthrough won't hurt the experience much (it is wise to lock it until the game is completed for the first time). There were some spelling (Episode 3; objective; "motiviation") and grammar mistakes, but those are minor issues. Apart from these, there aren't much things which I'd want to be added to this game. 

I've written too much for this review already and thus will conclude my overall impression for the game. The game is truly amazing BUT is not for everyone. If you crave for action and excitement and don't like reading and analyzing, then I do not recommend this game to you. But hey! It's never a bad time to explore a new frontier and discover a little bit more about yourself. Maybe you'll love this game the same as I did and give it a thumbs up.
